steps.say: One baby in five thousand is born with the back passage ending blind instead of opening on the skin. Boys slightly outnumber girls, and the commonest patterns are a channel into the urinary bulb in boys and a channel into the vaginal entrance in girls.
steps.tx: **Imperforate anus** (blind back passage) occurs in **1** (one) in **5000** (five thousand) births with **58** (fifty eight) percent male, spanning perineal groove to **cloaca** (common channel), with **rectobulbar urethral fistula** (bowel-to-urine channel) commonest in males and **rectovestibular** (bowel-to-vaginal-entrance) commonest in females.

steps.say: In the sixth week a wall divides the common chamber into bowel behind and urinary tract in front, and a membrane covering the anal pit later dissolves. When the wall fails, bowel joins the urinary tract; when the membrane fails, the opening sits too far forward or narrows. A three-centimetre common channel marks the short-to-long cloaca line, guiding repair.
steps.tx: The **urorectal septum** (dividing wall) divides the **cloaca** (common chamber) by week **6** (six) and the **anal membrane** (pit cover) resorbs, so septum failure gives bowel to urinary fistulas and membrane failure gives stenosis or anterior perineal openings. A **cloaca** (fused rectum, vagina and urethra) with a **3** (three) cm channel marks short versus long defects. A single female orifice means cloaca, and two orifices suggest **urogenital sinus** (dual channel) with normal anus.

steps.say: The backbone tells the future. Missing two or more sacral vertebrae predicts poor bowel and bladder control, and a tethered cord or fatty lump on the cord needs imaging. The diagram pairs these spinal defects with the rest of the associated anomalies.
steps.tx: **Sacral agenesis** (missing tailbone) and spinal defects affect a third (**33** (thirty three) percent) of patients, absent two or more vertebrae shapes **continence prognosis** (control outlook), and **tethered cord** (stuck spinal cord), **lipomeningocele** (fatty cord lump) and fatty **filum** (cord tail) need imaging. The spinal level sets expectations before any reconstruction.

vis.caption: VACTERL anomalies travel with anorectal malformations. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: The higher the defect, the more the kidneys suffer, requiring full urinary screening. Nine in ten cloaca and bladder-neck fistulas carry urinary defects with reflux and swelling commonest, against one in ten for the lowest openings. Ultrasound of the kidneys plus a bladder dye study plus heart and food-pipe screening are routine.
steps.tx: **Genitourinary anomalies** (kidney-urine defects) rise with defect height to **90** (ninety) percent in cloaca and rectovesical fistula but only **10** (ten) percent in perineal fistula, with **vesicoureteral reflux** (backflow) and **hydronephrosis** (swollen kidneys) commonest. Renal **ultrasound** (kidney scan) and voiding **cystourethrogram** (bladder dye study) are routine plus echo and orogastric tube for cardiac and oesophageal associations.

steps.say: The drawing shows the classic high defect: a blind rectal pouch joined to the urinary channel with no anal opening on the skin. Low perineal and vestibular channels go straight to single-stage repair, while this blind pouch with a urinary connection needs a stoma first. Reading the pouch level on the first film sets the whole plan.
steps.tx: **Blind rectal pouch** (sealed bowel end) with **rectourethral fistula** (bowel-urine join) and **imperforate perineum** (no anal opening) defines the high defect needing staged repair. **Perineal** (skin-level) and **vestibular fistulas** (vaginal-entrance channels) undergo single stage repair without stoma, while blind pouches and rectourinary fistulas need a divided **sigmoid colostomy** (bowel stoma) with mucous fistula first.

vis.caption: Blind rectal pouch with rectourethral fistula and imperforate perineum. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Definitive repair pulls the bowel down through the muscle ring under electrical mapping. The surgeon stimulates the fibres to find the centre of the sphincter before placing the bowel, usually between three and six months of age after the stoma. The distal bowel dye study outlines the fistula, guiding the pull-through.
steps.tx: **Posterior sagittal anorectoplasty** (muscle-splitting pull-through) at **3** (three) to **6** (six) months places bowel through the mapped **sphincter** (control muscle) after a divided colostomy, guided by a distal **colostogram** (stoma dye study) that maps the fistula. **Electrical sphincter mapping** (muscle stimulation) centres the pull-through.

steps.say: The new opening must be stretched on schedule or it scars shut. Dilatations start two weeks after repair and continue for months past closure, and even a normally placed but narrow anus answers to serial stretching alone. Parents learn the routine before discharge, practising daily.
steps.tx: **Anal dilatations** (stretching routine) start **2** (two) weeks after anorectoplasty and continue months past closure, and a normally placed **anal stenosis** (narrow opening) is managed by serial dilation or **cutback anoplasty** (opening enlargement) alone. Stopping early invites **stricture** (scar narrowing).

steps.say: Dryness is not the goal; social continence is. Three quarters of children achieve voluntary bowel movements, reaching social continence, though half of those still soil between movements. Constipation remains the commonest aftermath, managed with a bowel programme of softeners and washouts rather than repeated surgery.
steps.tx: **Social continence** (school-ready control) is the goal with **75** (seventy five) percent achieving voluntary bowel movements though half of those still show **soiling** (staining), defining **fecal continence** (bowel control) as the goal. **Constipation** (hard infrequent stools) remains the commonest sequela, needing a **bowel management** (washout programme) of softeners and **laxatives** (stool looseners).
